other_side: NLW's enterprise picture is reassuring. Business leaders shrug at extinction risk, spend on agent security and owned models, and the Ramp dip in top-1% spending per employee from $8,000 to $7,200 a month mostly reflects price cuts and seasonality. Zitron's Concentration Risk, ten days earlier, reads the same Ramp data very differently. By his account 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic's enterprise revenue comes from 1% of customers, a share that has not improved in three years. That top 1% skews heavily towards tech companies and AI startups that resell subsidised tokens using venture money, which he calls 'the NINJA borrowers of the AI era'. On this view the 'real' enterprises, where software money is usually made, are not spending much on AI at all. He also flags the risk that NLW treats as opportunity: those same heavy spenders are the customers most likely to leave for cheaper open-source or self-hosted models. Every move towards owned models is therefore revenue walking away from the labs, whose take-or-pay compute commitments, he argues, behave like debt that is owed whatever the demand.
truth_beneath: The question both men keep circling is who is actually paying for enterprise AI, and whether those payers will stay. Both rely on Ramp. Both accept that spending is concentrated in a small, tech-heavy group, that customers switch vendors easily, and that owned and open-weight models are becoming a serious alternative, as Latham and Watkins buying its own servers shows. The question that will settle it is whether spending spreads beyond the top 1% into banks, insurers, law firms and health systems at real prices. The thing to look for is the concentration figure itself: whether Ramp's 80% share from 1% of customers falls over the next two quarters as ordinary businesses scale up, or holds while top-tier spending keeps slipping. What remains is worldview. NLW reads vendor churn and owned models as a maturing market. Zitron reads them as the labs' best customers leaving. NLW is vindicated if non-tech enterprises start writing large cheques to labs and to agent-security vendors. Zitron is vindicated if the dip in top-1% spending turns into a trend while the compute bills keep arriving. Both are polemicists with incentives, NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both see a customer base that is shifting, not settled. Watch Ramp's next index.
